## The problem

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](../images/rasters_vs_distributions.png){width="80%"}
:::



## Why this matters for raster data

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](../images/rasters_everywhere.png){width="90%"}
:::


## Current gap

Distribution plots are common in R:

- `ggplot2`
- `ggridges`
- `ggdist`
- `plotly`

But they are mostly designed for **tabular data**.

::: {.takehome}
Raster users often need custom scripts to convert rasters into data frames before visualization.
:::

## Aim of the framework

::: {.large-center}
Create a unified workflow for **distribution-based visualization of geographical rasters** directly in R.
:::

The framework is implemented in the open-source package:

::: {.package}
`imageRy`
:::

available at:
<https://github.com/ducciorocchini/imageRy>


::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](../images/imageRy.png){width="20%"}
:::

## Three complementary functions

| Function | Purpose |
|-----------|---------|
| `im.ridgeline()` | Compare distributions among raster layers |
| `im.boxplot.layers()` | Compare medians, spread and densities among layers |
| `im.boxplot.classes()` | Compare distributions among spatial classes |
|||

Together, these functions provide a comprehensive **framework for distribution-based exploration** of raster data.

# 1. Global exploration

## Global exploration

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](../images/im_ridgeline.png){width="80%"}
:::


## Empirical example: monthly NDVI

```{r echo=T}
library(terra)
ls <- list.files(
  "~/Documents/ridgeline_plots/perduccio/ndvi",
  pattern = "\\.tif$",
  full.names = TRUE
)
ndvi <- rast(ls)
plot(ndvi)
```

## Ridgelines reveal the seasonal signal

```{r, echo=T}
library(imageRy)
im.ridgeline(ndvi, scale=2, palette="viridis")
```

## Names

```{r, echo=T}
names(ndvi) <- c("01-Jan", "02-Feb", "03-Mar", "04-Apr", "05-May", "06-Jun", "07-Jul", "08-Aug", "09-Sep", "10-Oct", "11-Nov", "12-Dec") 
im.ridgeline(ndvi, scale=2, palette="viridis")
```

## Scale
```{r, echo=T}
names(ndvi) <- c("01-Jan", "02-Feb", "03-Mar", "04-Apr", "05-May", "06-Jun", "07-Jul", "08-Aug", "09-Sep", "10-Oct", "11-Nov", "12-Dec") 
im.ridgeline(ndvi, scale=4, palette="viridis")
```

## 3. Class-wise distribution

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](../images/classwise.png){width="80%"}
:::

## Empirical example: drone imagery

```{r, echo=T}
canale <- rast("~/Documents/lectures_and_seminars/images/canale_aquila.JPG")
plot(canale)
```

## Empirical example: classified image

```{r, echo=T}
classcanale <- im.classify(canale, num_clusters=4)
```


## Empirical example: final kernel-density boxplot

```{r, echo=T, eval=FALSE}
library(imageRy)
im.boxplot.classes(canale, classcanale, density=TRUE, layer=1)
```

::: {style="text-align: center;"}
![](../images/boxplotclasses.png){width="40%"}
:::


## Methodological contribution

The framework provides a progressive workflow:

::: {.flow}
`SpatRaster` → `im.ridgeline()` → `im.boxplot.layers()` → `im.classify()` → `im.boxplot.classes()`
:::

It integrates:

- **raster-native** workflows
- **reproducible R code**

## Coda

Distribution-based visualization complements map-based analysis by showing information that maps often hide.

The framework helps users move from:

1. **global distribution** exploration
2. statistically informed **layer comparison**
3. spatially explicit **class-wise interpretation**

::: {.takehome}
The main value is not a single plot, but a coherent exploratory workflow for raster data.
:::
